43: Prodigal God Tim Keller America North America Non-Fiction Christian Faith 2013 2008

First off, as an English major I am embarrassed to admit that I did not know the correct definition of the word prodigal. I always thought it referred to someone who screws up and comes back around, hat in hand. I couldn't be further from the truth — prodigal means someone who is wastefully extravagant, who spends their resources recklessly and freely. So in this story what you really have is a parable about two lost sons and a reckless (with his love) father. Keller's reorientation of the story from its traditional focus on the wayward son gives one more accurate insight into just who this tale was for. In context, Jesus' main audience was the 'older brothers' — the self-righteous pharisees who sought to control their own salvation through rigorous adherence to the law. One of best parts of Prodigal God is that it turns the reader outward showing that recognition of God's costly grace should spur his followers to serve the poor, to love the orphans and widows in society today. On my yearly re-reading list. ¶ The targets of the [prodigal son story] are not wayward sinners but religious people who do everything the Bible requires.

It's one of those rare books that spreads its tentacles around you, the reader, and refuses to release you. ¶ To be in Africa you have to be strong. We're not strong. We don't even have a flag.
92: A Grief Observed C.S. Lewis England Europe Christian Christian Faith 2016 1961

Lewis recounts an honest and open account of one man's reckoning with the loss of his wife--tragically he only had a few short years with her before she died after a battle with cancer. This is one of those books that you hope you never have to be glad you read. What makes this short book special is Lewis' honesty, as his wife's death causes him to question everything that he believes, including his own faith. Ultimately, Lewis emerges from his sorrow with a deepened faith.
93: All Our Names Dinaw Mengestu Uganda Africa Fiction Africa Sweeping Fiction 2016 2014

Read It Because it will Break Your Heart. And it's the Great African Novel. As I read through the final pages of the novel and watched the final paragraphs fade away my heart began to ache and break because I didn't want to let the characters go. And then I focused and slowly read through the final line. I won't ruin it for you but that line — oh that line — it will break your heart. ¶ No one needs to learn how to kill, but it took the foreigners who came to Africa to show us that it meant nothing to do so.
94: Allah is Not Obliged Ahmadou Kourouma Côte d'Ivoire Africa Fiction Africa Conflict Zones & Hard Truths 2016 2000

Well, it's hard to say that you 'love' a book about child soldiers, but Kourouma has crafted a first person narrative that is brutal and funny. Allah is Not Obliged is the tale of a young Ivorian boy named Birahima who becomes a child soldier of misfortune, killing and pontificating his way across West Africa. The best portions of the novel are the quasi histories of the different countries--Kourouma boils down the essential tenets of the political and warfield battles in an easy to read and digestible manner. ¶ Allah is not obliged to be fair about everything, about all his creations, about all his actions here on earth.
95: An African in Greenland Tété-Michel Kpomassie Greenland, Togo Africa Biography Africa Christian Faith 2016 1981

It was unlike anything I've ever read. This is the fantastical post-independence autobiographical tale of a young Togolese boy that leaves his 25 siblings on a whim (basically) and starts a 12-year journey from his native country to the chilly northern reaches of Greenland. It all started after he saw a book on Greenland in a missionary book store in his village.
96: Ghana Must Go Taiye Selasi Ghana Africa Fiction Africa Sweeping Fiction 2016 2013

This is not a novel about Africa, or Ghana, or Nigeria or immigrants (only), this is one of the classic novels about family, identity, loss, and forgiveness that follows you around in your idle thoughts long after you are finished. Selasi's mastery is most evident as she captures the sights, sounds and people of Ghana and Nigeria. The element that makes this such a timeless story is that it's ultimately about the power and indefatigability of a mother's love and hope. ¶ Death must take place in the heart to be believed in. After love dies man believes in his death.
97: Houseboy Ferdinand Oyono Cameroon Africa Fiction Africa Sweeping Fiction 2016 1956

Oyono crafts a beautiful, tragic and damning tale about being a "black Frenchman" in Cameroon. This question of identity is at the center of this tale of a houseboy named Toundi with hopes of assimilation and upward mobility. With his near-to-last dying words being the question, "What are we blackmen who are called French?", one gets the sense that it's not going to end well for the young man. ¶ I shall be the Chief European's boy. The dog of the King is the King of dogs.
98: I Did Not Come to You by Chance Adaobi Tricia Nwaubani Nigeria Africa Fiction Africa Sweeping Fiction 2016 2009

You'll finally get to know that Nigerian prince who has been emailing you! In her debut novel Nwaubani follows in the footsteps of Adichie as she pulls back the curtain on the 419 industry in Nigeria--those oddly written emails from a Nigerian prince or businessman who needs your help to access a windfall. With an eye for humor and for heart, Nwaubani crafts a classic tragedy that follows the rise of Kingsley as he ascends a 419 crime syndicate, humanizing him as he becomes more and more adept at swindling gullible mugus. ¶ The past is constraining but the future has no limits.
99: In Praise of Savagery Warwick Cairns Ethiopia Africa Non-Fiction Biography Memoir & a Life Examined 2016 2010

You will learn about the incredible journeys that the original European adventurers made as they explored the previously "undiscovered" interior of Africa. In Praise of Savagery is the memoir of a young man who befriended the great British explorer Wilfred Thesiger. Eventually, Cairns gets the opportunity to essentially retrace Thesiger's original steps when he first set out to find the origin of the Awash River in Ethiopia. ¶ The point is this. Wilfred Thesiger was a man who made a difference to the world.
100: Leaving Tangier Tahar Ben Jelloun Morocco Africa Fiction Africa Sweeping Fiction 2016 2006

This was a sad, tragic, beautifully written tale about loneliness, despair, hope and home--in other words, it encompasses the entire range of the human condition that you expect a great novel to cover. Leaving Tangier stands the test of time as I read it ten years after its publication. It's a timely tale about the harsh reality of immigration and emigration and the depths that desperation drives one to. ¶ Exile revealed the true dimensions of calamity.
101: Parenting with Love and Logics Charles Fay and Foster Clin America North America Non-Fiction Leadership & Building Things 2016 1990

You want to come up with a systematic approach to raise your kids into adults with healthy self-esteem who have the skills to make wise decisions for themselves. The authors divide your conflict interactions with kids into two broad categories: ones that affect you in some way, and those that affect your kids only--the latter requires a more deft touch where you allow your kids to experience the consequences of a poor decision, WITH EMPATHY. ¶ I love you too much to argue with you about this.
102: Salvage the Bones Jesmyn Ward Mississippi North America Fiction Sweeping Fiction 2016 2011

You will be reminded of both the devastating scope and power of Hurricane Katrina but also of the largely forgotten swathes of the American population. Jesmyn Ward creates a world and captures its dialogue and cultural inner monologue with a level of detail and tenderness that will keep its characters alive in your thoughts long after you've finished the novel. Ward's artistry is most strikingly displayed in how she somehow manages to humanize a character that dogfights his nursing pitbull. ¶ Katrina is the mother we will remember until the next mother with large, merciless hands, committed to blood, comes.
103: Ships of Mercy Don Stephens America North America Non-Fiction Leadership & Building Things 2016 2005

You will see the transformation of a dream into the reality of millions of lives changed forever. Don Stephens' story is an incredible one--that Mercy Ships is the successful organization that it is today is nothing short of a miracle. A man had a dream to one day have a fleet of hospital ships that provide free surgeries to the poorest nations in the world. Today Mercy Ships has already served millions and is set to serve even more. ¶ They become a nonperson, hiding in the bush, shunned, literally waiting to die.
104: So Long a Letter Mariama Bâ Senegal Africa Fiction Africa Sweeping Fiction 2016 1979

Read it because you get to peer into the birth of feminism for a Muslim woman in post-independence Senegal. It took me a little bit to get into this story, mainly because I'd never read a book whose format was a simple, lengthy meandering letter. Ultimately, Ba won me over with her tender, thoughtful introspective look at the life of a cuckolded, then sister-wifed, then widowed, then independent and finally (maybe) free woman. ¶ Friendship has splendours that love knows not.
105: Stories John Armstrong America North America Non-Fiction Memoir & a Life Examined 2016 2010

Unfortunately, Armstrong has chosen not to try to publish his striking memoir of short vignettes that span the course of his memorable life. The depth of this level of emotional honesty laid bare on the pages are unlike anything I've ever read.
106: Superforecasting Philip E. Tetlock and Dan M. Gardner America North America Non-Fiction Leadership & Building Things 2016 2015
107: The Girl on the Train Paula Hawkins England Europe Fiction Sweeping Fiction 2016 2015

You can finish it in three days (or in one day at the beach), it's that fast of a read. Aside from being a pretty dark novel this is a perfect beach read. This story touches upon all the major nerves: falling in love, betrayal, jealousy, depression, murder, delusion--you get it all. Hawkins does a great job masking the outcome from the reader--this is the pull that keeps the pages turning. ¶ Nobody warned me it would break us. But it did.
108: The Jive Talker or How to Get a British Passport Samson Kambalu Malawi, England Africa Fiction Africa Sweeping Fiction 2016 2008

Kambalu is a gifted and funny writer who presents his life, and that of his father the Jive Talker, as an open book. Technically this isn't fiction but this Malawian Banda-era coming-of-age tale sure reads like it. In the tale, the 'jive talker' is the author's hustling alcoholic father who was known to riff bombastically on an encyclopedic range of subjects, a trait that obviously wore off on his son. ¶ Holyballism is a state of mind.
109: The Kafir of Khartala Mohamed Toihiri Comoros Africa Fiction Africa Sweeping Fiction 2016 1984

Unfortunately, there is no published English version of this novel--I was only able to read it because I asked for a copy from the professor who had translated it at the University of Vermont. Published in 2000 amidst one of Comoros' many coups, Toihiri has penned a wry, surprisingly racy novel that satirizes much of the politics and culture of his home country. At the heart of the story is a married doctor's affair with a younger French NGO teacher, and the doctor is dying from cancer.
110: The Sympathizer Viet Thanh Nguyen Vietnam Asia Fiction War, Service & Sacrifice 2016 2015

You get to view the Vietnam War from a totally different perspective--in this case, that of a South Vietnamese officer who is actually an American-educated spy for the communist North. Other themes addressed against the backdrop of the war include poverty, Hollywood "yellow-washing," torture, love-making and billiards, confession, forgetting and happiness as a zero-sum game in war.
111: They Are Coming Christopher Mlalazi Zimbabwe Africa Fiction Africa Sweeping Fiction 2016 2014

You are wanting to read something from Zimbabwe. Look, this wasn't the best thing I've ever read but it was an important read because it forced me to think of the idea of family outside the normal western version. In this story a township family struggles as a rebellious daughter joins a local militia before the approaching 2005 parliamentary elections--it's about the locality of all politics but more so about what it means to grow up amidst uncertainty and violence. ¶ When we're very frightened we can do the impossible.
112: Through the Eyes of a Lion Levi Lusko America North America Non-Fiction Memoir & a Life Examined 2016 2015

This is a book about unspeakable loss but it's also a book that offers you a plan--not only for yourself but also for comforting others. This is one of those books that you might not really want to read for fear of some type of psychic pain by association, but you will be glad you did.
113: American Rust Philipp Meyer America North America Fiction Sweeping Fiction 2017 2009

I first encountered Meyer's writing back in 2015 by way of S.C. Gwynne's incredible Empire of the Summer Moon, which led me to Meyer's The Son. That led me to Meyer's first novel, American Rust, which reads like a sorrowful swan song to the American rust belt, drawing the reader into the lives of several families struggling to love, survive, and escape as the steel industry dies around them. My only critique is that I wished Meyer had wrapped up the story a little more neatly. ¶ You ought to be able to grow up in a place and not have to get the hell out of it when you turn eighteen.
114: Artemis Andy Weir America North America Fiction Sci-Fi Sci-Fi & Dystopian 2017 2017

I read author Andy Weir's blockbuster debut novel The Martian back in 2015 and loved it, so when Artemis came out I added it to my Audible queue. Artemis is a colony on the moon, and the story focuses on a young smuggler named Jazz, raised on the moon, who develops a pirat-ish code of conduct aimed at moving up the stratified social order. Jazz irked me at times--she comes across as a little too enamored with just how cute and clever she is--but Weir has done what talented authors do: create a previously unknown world and open its door to readers everywhere.
115: Chaos Monkeys Antonio García Martínez America North America Non-Fiction Business Leadership & Building Things 2017 2016

Chaos Monkeys is a book bulging with so much saucy insider detail that you feel a little guilty reading it. Readers will find it of particular value if they are looking to get into the weeds of starting their own company, launching an idea, or courting investors. Beyond that, there was much lacking in Martinez' life choices in my personal opinion--don't expect to finish the book feeling great about the story, which is more an indictment of the rather sordid way things are done in Silicon Valley than of the author himself. ¶ Love is grand, but hate and fear last longer.
116: Deep Work Cal Newport America North America Non-Fiction Business Leadership & Building Things 2017 2016

This was one of the most useful books that I have ever read. My full review is titled 'Read Deep Work Because It Will Change Everything.' ¶ Great creative minds think like artists but work like accountants.
117: Essentialism: The Discipline Pursuit of Less Greg McKeown America North America Non-Fiction Leadership & Building Things 2017 2014

Essentialism is a book for anyone who feels overwhelmed at any level of their life. The author's contention is that we all have too much going on in our lives, at work, at play, in our relationships and in our things, and this book gives the reader the tools and philosophical background to pare away the excess. Ultimately, McKeown espouses the expansion of designer Dieter Ram's mantra "less but better" into one's life at every level. ¶ You cannot overestimate the unimportance of practically everything.
118: Hawaii James A. Michener America North America Fiction Historical Fiction Sweeping Fiction 2017 1959

In 2009, I married my beautiful bride on Poipu Beach in Kauai, and since then the Hawaiian islands have held a special place in my heart. First published in 1959, Hawaii comes across a little dated in style but Michener nonetheless proves he can craft an engrossing tale as he spans the physical birth of the Hawaiian islands eons ago up to its fight for statehood, juxtaposing generations of earnest missionaries with lusty whalers and traders. One assumes Michener took a multitude of historical liberties, but upon finishing it I was okay with that. ¶ It is difficult to be king when the gods are changing.
119: Hidden Christmas Tim Keller America North America Non-Fiction Christian Christian Faith 2017 2016

Tim Keller stepped down as senior pastor at the renowned Redeemer Church in NYC in early 2017, the church he built into 5000 strong members in one of the most unchurched areas of the United States. Hidden Christmas is the product of a lifetime of Keller's Christmas sermons, covering the breadth of the Christmas story from its roots in the Old Testament. I finished it with a newfound understanding for just how significant it was that God became man--that all that had to happen for the people of Israel to approach God was to merely come, and adore him, in a manger, as a defenseless baby. ¶ The manger at Christmas means that, if you live like Jesus, there won't be room for you in a lot of inns.
120: Moving the Palace Charif Majdalani Lebanon, Sudan Africa Fiction Africa Sweeping Fiction 2017 2007

Majdalani's Moving the Palace is one of those books that leaves you melancholy and blue because it's over, and your relationship with the protagonist is severed forever, buried in the pages of the novel. We learn the story of Samuel, an erudite Christian adventurer who leaves his homeland of Lebanon amidst the great migration of the early 20th century and ventures down to the Sudan, where he encounters a small Arabian palace and hatches a plan of an origin his grandson can only guess at. ¶ I do not know--nor will anyone, ever--what planted the seed of that incredible idea in his mind.
121: Prodigal God Tim Keller America North America Non-Fiction Christian Christian Faith 2017 2008

First off, as an English major I am embarrassed to admit that I did not know the correct definition of the word prodigal. I always thought it referred to someone who screws up and comes back around, hat in hand. I couldn't be further from the truth — prodigal means someone who is wastefully extravagant, who spends their resources recklessly and freely. So in this story what you really have is a parable about two lost sons and a reckless (with his love) father. Keller's reorientation of the story from its traditional focus on the wayward son gives one more accurate insight into just who this tale was for. In context, Jesus' main audience was the 'older brothers' — the self-righteous pharisees who sought to control their own salvation through rigorous adherence to the law. One of best parts of Prodigal God is that it turns the reader outward showing that recognition of God's costly grace should spur his followers to serve the poor, to love the orphans and widows in society today. On my yearly re-reading list. ¶ Prodigal means someone who is wastefully extravagant, who spends their resources recklessly and freely. ¶ The targets of the [prodigal son story] are not wayward sinners but religious people who do everything the Bible requires.
122: Sleepwalking Land Mia Couto Mozambique Africa Fiction Africa Sweeping Fiction 2017 1992

Mia Couto has crafted a surreal, engrossing tragic tale of the hopelessness of life during the fifteen year long civil war that consumed post-independence Mozambique. Couto focuses on pulling the reader into the psyche of those affected most by war--the ones not doing the killing--the women and the children. Early on, the narrator relates one of the most bizarre stories I've ever read: his younger brother is forced to live in the family's henhouse by their insane father, and forced to act like a chicken, for so long that he eventually becomes one and disappears. ¶ Dreams are letters we send to our other, remaining lives.
123: The Hard Thing About Hard Things Ben Horowitz America North America Non-Fiction Business Leadership & Building Things 2017 2014

This book is on just about every entrepreneur's reading list. While much of the discussion is tech-focused, it would serve most military leaders well because Horowitz devotes much of his time to addressing how best to cope with the loneliness of leadership and "command." The most useful section for me came in chapter five: "Take Care of the People, The Products, and the Profits, In That Order." For any military leader planning to transition to the civilian workforce, this book should feature prominently on his or her reading list prior to retirement. ¶ Take Care of the People, The Products, and the Profits, In That Order.
124: The Last Will and Testament of Senor da Silva Araujo Germano Almeida Cape Verde Africa Fiction Africa Sweeping Fiction 2017 1989

This translated piece of Cape Verdean fiction is beautiful, sad, and meandering as it examines the life of a poor peasant boy made good as a successful business owner. Senor da Silva's life unfolds in a non-linear, often-dreamlike fashion as we follow him through the reading of his last will and testament. Far more interesting, though, is the investigation by da Silva's illegitimate daughter into a mysterious love obsession named Adelia. As the details are slowly revealed, a melancholy shadow falls over da Silva as he grapples with love, rejection and loss.
125: The Leader's Bookshelf Adm. James Stavridis & R. Manning Ancell America North America Non-Fiction Leadership & Building Things 2017 2017

Jim Stavridis' gift to bookavores everywhere, The Leader's Bookshelf is difficult to take notes on because it's so packed with great and essential material. Stavridis and former Navy PAO R. Ancell put together a Top 50 reading list for military leaders by surveying hundreds of senior military leaders, then ranked the most frequently cited titles by frequency of citation. As a FAO, I enjoyed Stavridis' analyses that repeatedly noted the need for regional expertise to better inform national strategic decision-making. ¶ Outside solutions unanchored by an understanding of a given regional system are almost always doomed to fail.
126: The Twelve Lives of Samuel Hawley Hannah Tinti America North America Fiction Sweeping Fiction 2017 2017

Let me just get it out of the way and say that Chapter 15 will break your heart. The Twelve Lives of Samuel Hawley is a modern day adaptation of the ancient Greek tale of the 12 Labors of Hercules, and the genius of author Hannah Tinti's story is that she layers several tragic love stories onto this epic framework. Mechanically, the novel overlays the history of the 12 bullets that struck Samuel Hawley during his life with his daughter Lou's own coming of age, as she slowly uncovers her father's sordid criminal past. ¶ Everything breaks if you hit it hard enough.
127: The Warmth of Other Suns Isabel Wilkerson America North America Non-Fiction African-American Conflict Zones & Hard Truths 2017 2010

Read it Because: You can't afford not to. Before the publication of Warmth some seven years ago, there had never been a definitive and comprehensive analysis of these waves of migration that began following the reconstruction era as Jim Crow set in. Let the following statement sink in: Just 77 years ago, in 1/3 of the US, killing blacks was not a crime. Now while I may not agree with every single tenet of the #blacklivesmatter movement, reading this book opened my eyes to the historical headspace from which its leaders and followers are coming. Much of the conflict in today's society would at least be softened if both sides took the time to know one another's history. Wilkerson has presented a gift to Americans. ¶ 'Sometimes,' he said, 'you have to stoop to conquer.' ¶ Most of them care nothing whatsoever about race. They want only their proper place in the sun and the right to be left alone, like any other citizen of the republic.
128: Transit Abdourahman A. Waberi* Djibouti Africa Fiction Africa Sweeping Fiction 2017 2003

As you can probably guess there's not exactly a ton of Djibouti fiction out there, especially en anglais, but when it comes to Djibouti fiction, the author Waberi reigns supreme. Transit interweaves the story of Bashir, an uneducated ex-soldier, with that of Harbi, a member of the opposition intellectual elite, as the two men reveal their life stories while waiting at the Paris airport. The staying power of this story comes from Waberi's deft touch as he tackles the complexity of his country's history and current political situation through alternating monologues. ¶ I'm the product of love without borders; I'm a hyphen between two worlds.
129: Vakio Milamina Soamiely Andriamananjara Madagascar Africa Fiction Africa Sweeping Fiction 2017 2012

It gives you the inside scoop on the culture and politics of Madagascar. Soamiely is the rare Malagasy author who writes in (great) English about these things. Vakio Milamina lays out the author's thoughts on life in Madagascar through a series of very loosely related essays. In particular I loved "It's All Part of Growing Up," basically a 6 page rundown on the political history of Madagascar, and "Our Unambiguously Ambiguous Art of Conversation," in which he lays out why a Malagasy will seldom ever say 'no.'
130: African Kaiser Robert Gaudi Tanzania Africa Non-Fiction Africa War, Service & Sacrifice 2018 2017

It quickly becomes apparent in this impressive tome that author Robert Gaudi is a bit of a von Lettow-Vorbeck fanboy, but the admiration isn't without merit--the reader learns of the insurmountable odds faced by the German general fighting alone, without logistical support, in German East Africa during World War I. He ended his four-year struggle in unconditional surrender, but completed his military service as a victor, having pushed Great Britain to expend immense treasure and forces pursuing his small army of guerrilla fighters. This lengthy book flies by on the strength of Gaudi's story-telling.
131: American War: A Novel Omar El Akkad America North America Fiction Sci-Fi & Dystopian 2018 2017

Egyptian-Canadian journalist-turned-author Omar El Akkad has penned a tale of future-historical fiction, dropping us into a world 40 years from now where America has erupted into conflict over the federal government's outlawing of fossil fuels, aggravated by accelerated global warming and rising ocean levels. We witness the tragic arc of Sarat, a young girl whose life is thrown into chaos as war encroaches on her family, and who becomes a hardened sniper, then prisoner of war, then mass murderer. The novel's staying power comes from Akkad's mastery in capturing how media and political rhetoric can distort reality and inflame a populace.
132: Beyond the Rice Fields Naivo Madagascar Africa Fiction Africa Conflict Zones & Hard Truths 2018 2012

Malagasy author Naivo has crafted a heart-wrenching tale of love set amidst one slave's seemingly impossible yearning for success and upward mobility. Impressively, this expansive piece of pre-colonial historical fiction doesn't hold back in addressing taboo subjects in Madagascar such as slavery and the wholesale execution of Christians under Queen Ranavalona's reign in the 19th century. The book reads as a mixture of hainteny (oral tale/poetry) and tantara (historical narrative) with a liberal dosing of Malagasy proverbs--I counted 29 of them. ¶ Love is like rice, when you transplant it, it grows, but never in the same way.
133: Dancing in the Glory of Monsters Jason Stearns DRC Africa Non-Fiction Africa Conflict Zones & Hard Truths 2018 2011

I listened to this lengthy journalistic endeavor by writer Jason Stearns as he attempts to unravel the most complicated conflict the world never cared about: the two wars in the Congo. As Stearns digs deeper you are quickly struck by the overwhelming intensity of violence--the sheer level of sexual violence is incomprehensible, and there's likely no one in the country of 64 million who doesn't know someone who was raped or assaulted. Ultimately, it is the absence of any justice or effective state institutions that marks the Congo's conflicts as distinct from those elsewhere in Africa. ¶ Who has not been Mobutists in this country? We saw you all, dancing in the glory of the monster.
134: Every Good Endeavor: Connecting Your Work to God's Work Tim Keller America North America Non-Fiction Christian Christian Faith 2018 2012

Pastor Tim Keller's Every Good Endeavor is not a beach read--it's a hunker-down-with-a-highlighter-and-pen examination of what work means to God and what it should mean to anyone following God, laying out the Bible's answers to why we want to work, why it's so hard, and how the story of Jesus' life leads us to find satisfaction in it. Ultimately, Keller argues that more than any marches, protests, or online petitions, our work is our greatest opportunity to shape culture. ¶ An idol is a good thing turned into an ultimate thing.
135: Memoirs of a Porcupine Alain Mabanckou Republic of Congo Africa Fiction Africa Sweeping Fiction 2018 1998

This is a difficult novel from renowned author Alain Mabanckou. Hailing from the Republic of Congo, Mabanckou has penned a pointed tale aimed at taking down the role of backwoods superstition amidst modernity--at least that's what really smart people say he was doing. I will admit I didn't really understand the point of this novel and had to do some research to come to that conclusion. I was pretty disappointed I hadn't picked a different Congolese novel, but I later discovered the book won the 2006 Renaudot prize, so I've decided to give it a second chance, at least on an intellectual level. ¶ I cling to my memories as the elephant clings to his tusks.
136: Sing, Unburied, Sing Jesmyn Ward America North America Fiction Sweeping Fiction 2018 2017

Early on, the young son of a barely-there, back-country, voodoo-meth-addicted mother makes the damning pronouncement that his mother "kills things," and indeed death hangs heavy in this novel. Ostensibly, this is a fairly straightforward narrative: a single mother, her two children, and her junkie friend embark on a road trip to pick up her boyfriend when he gets out of jail. The story's depth emerges as Ward reveals that three of the characters can see wandering dead ghosts looking for answers, and she's created characters with whom she so deeply empathizes that their visions seem real and necessary rather than fantastical. ¶ It feels good to be mean, to speak past the baby I can't hit.
137: The Beautiful Things that Heaven Bears Dinaw Mengestu Ethiopia Africa Fiction Africa Sweeping Fiction 2018 2007

Before Adichie was regaling the world with her story of a relatively privileged immigrant experience in 'Americanah', Ethiopian author Dinaw Mengestu was pulling back the curtain on a much bleaker immigrant experience. The title comes from the closing lines of Dante's Inferno. In the case of the narrator Sepha and his friends, they have escaped the violence in their own country and arrived in America, 'seeing the stars.' Only they soon discover that while their new life in the United States may not be hell, it will likely be much more like the penance of purgatory than that of paradiso. ¶ As it was, I did not come to America to find a better life. I came here running and screaming with the ghosts of an old one firmly attached to my back. ¶ All the best dictators are colonels.
138: The Gunny Sack M.G. Vassanji Tanzania Africa Fiction Africa Sweeping Fiction 2018 1989

Most of the African fiction that I've read has focused on the "native" experience, so I found this to be an important novel as it focuses exclusively on the experience of four generations of an Indian family in Tanzania and wider East Africa beginning in the late 1800s. Vassanji relates this in-depth experience across the span of Tanzania's colonization and eventual independence through the backward lens of the narrator Kala, who parses through the contents of a gunny sack bequeathed to him by his great grandmother.
139: The Memory of Love Aminattah Forna Sierra Leone Africa Fiction Africa Sweeping Fiction 2018 2010

"We all were happy here once," reminisces Kai, the local Freetown surgeon, after the death of his last link to the time before. With beautiful, striking prose, author Aminatta Forna reveals the soul of a nation where nearly everyone is stricken with what the West calls PTSD, but as one local notes, "You call it a disorder, my friend. We call it life." Forna does not give in to easy storylines about the courage of the war's survivors--it is the memory of Sierra Leone's before that gives people the strength to slowly put their lives together again. ¶ You call it a disorder, my friend. We call it life.
140: Turn the Ship Around David Marquet America North America Non-Fiction Leadership Leadership & Building Things 2018 2012

I let this book rest dormant on my Amazon wishlist for months because of my unfair bias against submariners, but I wasn't even a chapter in when I realized how misguided that bias had been. Midway through, retired Captain David Marquet shares the story of a nighttime passage through the strait of Malacca that nearly resulted in a collision, averted by the timely actions of one of his petty officers--whom Marquet immediately awarded a Navy Achievement Medal on the spot. This floored me, since in my own experience recognition like that almost always arrives a year late, if at all. ¶ Don't move information to authority, move authority to information.
141: What the Day Owes the Night Yasmina Khadra Algeria Africa Fiction Africa Sweeping Fiction 2018 2008

This book is a perfect example of why reading fiction is important. Reading fiction like this forces the reader to internalize and grapple with historical events in a way that a straightforward history never could. In this case, by personalizing something like the Algerian independence struggle, the reader must reevaluate the dry numbers, facts and statistics littering the historical record and connect them to the actual people and struggles behind them. ¶ Have you ever dared, Younes, even once in your life? ¶ If a woman loves you, no star is beyond your grasp, no god can touch you. ¶ Only love can make good the misfortunes and evils of the world.
142: Beacon 23 Hugh Howey America North America Fiction Sci-Fi Sci-Fi & Dystopian 2019 2015

Hugh Howey takes us for a ride with a PTSD'd alien-fighting grunt turned interstellar lighthouse keeper. Howey imagines a future in which "lighthouse beacons" are placed amidst warp speed preventing asteroid belts--lighthouse keepers control a device that, when activated, allows ships to pass through the asteroid belts without collision. Without that device activated, any passing ship will be obliterated. Couple this setting with a pending alien invasion and a possible love interest and you've got a great story you'll devour.
143: Beneath the Lion's Gaze Maaza Mengiste Ethiopia Africa Historical Fiction Conflict Zones & Hard Truths 2019 2010

One of the only African nations never to have been colonized, one of Ethiopia's darkest periods came during the 13-year socialist rule of the Derg. This military junta overthrew an increasingly oblivious Haile Selassie and set about consolidating power under the leadership of despot Mengistu, and Beneath the Lion's Gaze retells this period through the eyes of one Ethiopian family. The family's patriarch is a renowned doctor ordered to keep a barely-alive torture victim alive so she can be tortured further; his son becomes a freedom fighter known as "Mekonnen Killer of Soldiers." Author Maaza Mengiste uses this one family's struggles to bring to life the experience of Ethiopians who starved under Selassie, only to be persecuted and killed under the Derg and starved again under Mengistu's reign. ¶ Mekonnen Killer of Soldiers.
144: Between the World and Me Ta-Nehisi Coates America North America Biography African-American Memoir & a Life Examined 2019 2015

This is a love letter from a father to a son, written with the urgency of a man who knows he may perish at any moment. Coates writes beautifully as he recalls his youth and experiences as a father--his memoir reflects serious inner self-examination as he seeks to create a blueprint for his son to survive, and possibly even thrive, in a world Coates argues is stacked against him from a historical, institutional, and psycho-cultural perspective. As Coates warns his son to keep his guard up, he adds: "Never forget that we were enslaved in this country longer than we have been free." ¶ Never forget that we were enslaved in this country longer than we have been free.
145: Ghost Fleet P.W. Singer & August Cole America North America Fiction Military War, Service & Sacrifice 2019 2015

The premise is that sometime in the near future China, partnered with Russia, conducts a cyber/space/electronic warfare attack that gives them dominance across the warfare spectrum. Our fleet and air assets are near completely destroyed, and with all our U.S. satellites destroyed, the United States no longer has freedom of movement on land, air, or sea. The heart of the story is how the U.S. fights back--a combination of insurgency in the occupied Hawaiian islands, a reconstitution of mothballed ships and aircraft, a private-public wartime industrial partnership, and a murky collaboration with Anonymous hackers. The story moves quickly, and I burned through the pages as the authors keep the narrative moving with quick dialogue, myriad Sun-Tzu quotes, and sympathetic characters. ¶ We need to become again the country that breaks the hard problems, that sees the virtue in innovation and the reward in risk…
146: Gratitude in Low Voices Dawit Gebremichael Habte Eritrea Africa Historical Fiction Conflict Zones & Hard Truths 2019 2017

Equal parts memoir, history and adventure novel, Dawit Habte's book is the story of not only his country's 91-year struggle for independence but also his own incredible journey from a countryside village in Eritrea to the offices of Bloomberg as a software engineer. As with many refugee stories that have come out of Africa, the western reader will be floored by the tenacity, resilience and grit the author displays at such a young age as he smuggles himself out of Ethiopia and finally gets refugee status to start his life over in the United States. One thing that struck me was his commentary on the dehumanizing nature of seeking asylum--where you are assumed to be starting anew on a better life despite having a family, people, and country you call home half a world away. ¶ A refugee is always a pawn to be used.
147: Hillbilly Elegy J.D. Vance America North America Biography Memoir & a Life Examined 2019 2016

I read J.D. Vance's 2016 memoir of a family and culture in crisis in less than two days. Vance is just a flat-out great writer as he tells the story of his life growing up between Ohio and Kentucky along the redneck Rt. 23. His basic argument is that one of the major issues plaguing Appalachian America is that people there feel hopeless and disenfranchised, not just politically but in all facets of life--in short, they feel like their choices don't matter. In Vance's case, the only way he was able to rise above these circumstances was the reliable and persistent presence of a family member throughout his immediate family's tumultuous arc. Oh, that and a stint in the Marine Corps. ¶ The Marine Corps excised that feeling like a surgeon does a tumor.
148: Homegoing Yaa Gyasi Ghana Africa Fiction Sweeping Fiction 2019 2016

This masterpiece of historical fiction follows the lives of two separated half-sisters, and their six generations of descendants, beginning in the mid-1700s in the area of West Africa known today as Ghana. Gyasi uses their two very different paths to highlight not only the horrors of the slave trade but also the bravery and determination of the many who persevered and survived across the span of time. Ultimately, the 25-year-old author accomplishes a breath-taking feat in creating a compelling history of slavery told through 14 sequential short stories you'll likely never forget. ¶ We believe the one who has power. He is the one who gets to write the story.
149: Mister Drainpipe Marc Secchia Ethiopia Africa Fiction Africa Sweeping Fiction 2019

Author Marc Secchia took a hiatus from his slew of successful fantasy novels to pen this heartfelt love letter to the homeless of Addis Ababa. I tore through this book in less than two days, and I'll warn you that this story will pierce even the hardest heart and, hopefully, change the way you think about and interact with the homeless and "least" in your daily life. ¶ Every person, from the lowest to the highest, should be afforded dignity.
150: Prevail: The Inspiring Story of Ethiopia's Victory Over Mussolini's Invasion Jeff Pearce Ethiopia Africa Non-Fiction History Conflict Zones & Hard Truths 2019 2014

I can't imagine there's a more well-researched book out there on Ethiopia's decades-long resistance and eventual defeat of an overeager, over confident, overreaching wanna-be colonial power. Canadian author Jeff Pearce's work is strongest as he brings to life the myriad actors, antagonists, and heroes of the saga. It's worth noting that Pearce is a bit of a Selassie apologist, but given the complicated history of Ras Tafari Makkonen's reign, I imagine this can fall either way.
151: Rock Breaks Scissors William Poundstone America North America Non-Fiction Leadership & Building Things 2019 2014

The main point I took away from this novel was that people are crummy at trying to be "random." All of this book's applications are founded on one simple idea: when people make arbitrary, random, or strategic choices, they fall into unconscious patterns that you can predict. While entertaining to read, I'd say most of his writing is only useful for specific circumstances like taking multiple choice tests, office pools, rock-paper-scissors, catching fraud, and buying a home. ¶ When people make arbitrary, random, or strategic choices, they fall into unconscious patterns that you can predict.
152: Season of the Shadow Léonora Miano Cameroon Africa Fiction Sweeping Fiction 2019 2013

The story begins as the inhabitants of a tribal village tucked away in the interior of modern day Cameroon awaken to find its huts ablaze and 12 of its men vanished. This mysterious disappearance sets off a chain of events that, as one might guess, ends in tragedy. The tale's power comes as the reader is placed in the middle of a people group whose whole order and existence is thrown into havoc--even as the reader is keenly aware of what actually happened, the kidnapping is so out of place with centuries of accepted conduct that the village's own members can't fathom who the perpetrators might be. ¶ The shadow is also the shape our silences take.
153: The Shadow King Maaza Mengiste Ethiopia Africa Historical Fiction Sweeping Fiction 2019 2019

Following Mussolini's invasion to avenge Italy's 19th-century embarrassment at the Battle of Adua, Kidane assembles a local militia at exiled Emperor Haile Selassie's behest. His wife Aster leads the women who trail the fighters supplying food and bullets, and eventually convinces him to let her women fight. Mengiste brings to light a forgotten piece of Ethiopia's resistance against Italy — the women who fought and were written out of the history. Her talent has continued to grow since her debut, evident in stunning lines throughout. ¶ They have come to rewrite history, to alter memory, to resurrect their dead and refashion them as heroes. ¶ She is one woman. She is many women. She is all the sound that exists in the world. ¶ We were the Shadow King. We were those who stepped into a country left dark by an invading plague and gave new hope to Ethiopia's people.
154: Small Country Gaël Faye Burundi Africa Fiction Sweeping Fiction 2019 2016

Reading Gael Faye's Small Country, I was reminded of the writing of Teju Cole, Dinaw Mengestu, Maaza Mengiste, and NoViolet Bulawayo. Faye writes with a musician's flair, penning lines like "when he laughed, happiness washed over the walls of Mamie's small living room like a fresh lick of paint." Gabriel is Rwandan-French but spends his entire childhood in neighboring Burundi until the effects of the 1994 Rwanda genocide push him even further away to France, and it's there that he considers what exactly he's lost. ¶ I used to think I was exiled from my country. But, in retracing the steps of my past, I have understood that I was exiled from my childhood. Which seems so much crueler.
155: Strong Fathers, Strong Daughters: 10 Secrets Every Father Should Know Meg Meeker America North America Non-Fiction Christian Christian Faith 2019 2006

I first read this book back in 2015 and it's so important to fathers that I put it on my yearly re-reading list, although it took me four years to actually read it again. In my second reading it proved just as powerful, profound and insightful. The bottom line is that you can't underestimate the role of a father in his daughters' lives--you have to fight for her, engage with her, and continually draw her close throughout her life, particularly during those teen years. Don't worry about what other parents do; worry about your daughter. ¶ Dad, it’s not optional: your daughter needs you to be her hero.
156: The Dry Jane Harper Australia Asia Fiction Sweeping Fiction 2019 2016

In a dying Australian farm town, teetering on the edge of collapse due to droughts, a family is found dead in an apparent murder-suicide. An exiled man-turned-white-collar cop returns for the funeral and finds out his childhood best friend is the assumed killer of his own wife and kids. Did his friend do it? What secrets is the cop hiding? What secrets has the town buried? This was a page turner that kept me guessing till the end. A great quick read.
157: The Furious Longing of God Brennan Manning America North America Non-Fiction Christian Christian Faith 2019 2009

You can get through the 136 pages in one sitting if you'd like, but I think it's a book that's best consumed in spurts with time to mull over Brennan Manning's meditation on God's love for us. This book likely has a message for any reader, most importantly this: "Our religion never begins with what we do for God. It always starts with what God has done for us." ¶ Our religion never begins with what we do for God. It always starts with what God has done for us.
158: The Heart of War: Misadventures in the Pentagon Kathleen J. McInnis America North America Fiction Military War, Service & Sacrifice 2019 2018

McInnis' razor sharp, satirical story of a young, idealist, peacenik PhD's foray into the Pentagon brought me back to my days inside the 5-sided torture chamber. It's a novel about one woman's evolution from skeptic to true(ish) believer as she discovers that life inside is nothing like she expected. ¶ Applied to government, all things being equal, the stupidest explanation must be true.
159: The High Mountains of Portugal Yann Martel Portugal Europe Fiction Sweeping Fiction 2019 2016

Man Booker prize winning author Yann Martel has crafted a trio of related novellas that lay bare the trauma of loss and its psychic weight that can echo across generations like a deep curse. We join the journey of three characters: a bereaved widower on a mission to find a lost African crucifix; a grieving, delusional pathologist obsessed with Agatha Christie; and an aging widower/politician who buys a chimpanzee and retreats with the animal to his family's ancestral village. ¶ And now, how do I dare love anything?
160: The Three Body Problem Cixin Liu China Asia Fiction Sci-Fi Sci-Fi & Dystopian 2019 2006

This is a trippy novel that's not easily summarized, and it's easy to get lost in the more technical aspects that Cixin explores in depth (nanotechnology, AI, metaphysics, quantum mechanics), particularly when listening to it in 45 minute blocks on Audible in D.C. traffic over a month's time. The basic premise is that a technologically superior alien civilization has decided to colonize earth.
161: To Stop a Warlord: My Story of Justice, Grace, and the Fight for Peace Shannon Sedgwick Davis Uganda Africa Biography Conflict Zones & Hard Truths 2019 2019

This book is the story of how one woman created a new paradigm in how NGOs and charitable organizations should, could, and can confront atrocity and evil by partnering with the military. Shannon Davis is the CEO of Bridgeway Foundation, and she decided to do something about Joseph Kony and his reign of terror.
162: Where the Crawdads Sing Delia Owens America North America Fiction Sweeping Fiction 2019 2018

I read this beautiful lyrical book in two days, no exaggeration. It's equal parts murder mystery, searing social indictment, love letter to naturalism, and soaring poetry--amazing that this is author Delia Owens' first work of fiction. ¶ Go out as far as you can--way out yonder where the crawdads sing.
163: Where the Light Gets In: Losing My Mother Only To Find Her Again Kimberly Williams-Paisley America North America Biography Memoir Memoir & a Life Examined 2019 2016

A candid, emotional memoir of a daughter's struggles, hopes, triumphs, and losses as she copes with her mother's primary progressive aphasia, a rare form of dementia. The story is about more than the disease itself--it's about the bond between daughters and their mothers.
164: American Spy Lauren Wilkinson America North America Fiction Sweeping Fiction 2020 2019

This novel is both a fictionalized telling of Burkina Faso President Sankara's downfall and a commentary on what it means to be a black woman in both an American and African society. The protagonist is a black female FBI agent named Marie who is haunted by her sister's death and stifled by the lack of opportunity in her office. When she gets a chance to become a real spy she dives into it but soon realizes that many of her assumptions may have been wrong. ¶ That is what a woman's strength looks like when it's palatable: like she is containing herself.
165: Being Mortal Atul Gawande America North America Non-Fiction Memoir & a Life Examined 2020 2014

Early on author Atul Gawande captures the decision that we will all make (ideally) before we grow old: 'how to make life worth living when we're weak and frail and can't fend for ourselves anymore.' More specifically, he seeks to find out how people can age without having to choose between neglect and institutionalization. Most frightening is his conclusion that for the majority of the medical community 'hope is not a plan, but it is our plan.' ¶ Hope is not a plan, but it is our plan.
166: Blessed Child Ted Dekker & Bill Bright America North America Fiction Sweeping Fiction 2020 2001

The premise is that an American baby named Caleb is given to an Ethiopian monastery after his mother is murdered by invading Eritrean forces. Ten years later his life is in jeopardy and a Peace Corps worker and Red Cross nurse rescue him and take him to the U.S., where we discover that Caleb can heal people and that senior politicians want him dead. ¶ Whoever said that a straightened hand was more dramatic than a healed heart anyway?
167: Burn-In P.W. Singer & August Cole America North America Fiction Sweeping Fiction 2020 2020

In this future-historical fiction, the writing duo tackles a future in which AI, drones and robotics have continued their current development trajectory to the point where they've consumed every aspect of American life. Unfortunately, these "developments" have left gaping vulnerabilities within the US infrastructure that are exploited by a group of homegrown terrorists. ¶ Automation had always seemed a problem just for truck drivers or factory workers, until suddenly it wasn't.
168: By Night the Mountains Burn Juan Tomás Ávila Laurel Equatorial Guinea Africa Fiction Sweeping Fiction 2020 2009

This novel takes place during the colonial era on one of Equatorial Guinea's neglected islands--the country itself is run from its capital city Malabo on its largest island, Bioko. A frequent critic of dictator Obiang, the self-exiled author tells a tale of a marginalized community that survives, sometimes, on the narrowest of margins, depending on passing European ships and a strange periodic washing ashore of squids. ¶ Seeing is a form of taking part, and nobody can claim they didn't see it.
169: Call Sign Chaos Jim Mattis & Bing West America North America Non-Fiction War, Service & Sacrifice 2020 2019

This book has been long anticipated and it delivers. General Mattis writes just as he leads — candid and thoughtful. This book strikes a delicate balance between an autobiography and a leadership book. Mattis and co-author Bing West utilize Mattis' career as a roadmap to illustrate leadership at three different levels: Direct, Executive, and Strategic. The one theme he kept coming back to was unleashing others' initiative. Required reading for any military officer or anyone in a leadership position. ¶ Have a bias for action. Set the tempo for that action and reward those who meet that tempo or exceed it. Speed is king because time can't be recovered once it's lost. Reward the initiative of those under you--even when they fail.
170: Chasing Black Unicorns Marek Zmyslowski Poland, Nigeria Africa Non-Fiction Memoir & a Life Examined 2020 2019
171: Death Be Not Proud John Gunther America North America Non-Fiction Memoir & a Life Examined 2020 1949

The name of this 1949 memoir was taken from English poet John Donne's poem of the same title. In it the author and father John Gunther recounts the life and death of his son who passed after a struggle with a malignant brain tumor. ¶ A mournful tribute not only to Johnny but to the power, the wealth, the unconquerable beauty of the human spirit, will, and soul.
172: Designing Your Life: A Framework For Building A Life You Can Thrive In Bill Burnett & Dave Evans America North America Non-Fiction Leadership & Building Things 2020 2016

I also purchased the accompanying workbook which is excellent! The authors use design prototype theory to lead readers through a process of self-reflection and self-discovery. This is an ESSENTIAL read for any veteran considering a transition from the military, or for anyone considering a career pivot. ¶ Dysfunctional Belief: Happiness is having it all. Reframe: Happiness is letting go of what you don't need.
173: Diamonds, Gold, and War: The British, the Boers, and the Making of South Africa Martin Meredith South Africa Africa Non-Fiction Conflict Zones & Hard Truths 2020 2007

This book traces the origin of South Africa and the discovery of gold and diamonds there that sparked off a bloody conflict with Britain that ultimately led to the consolidation and foundation of the apartheid republic that existed until 1994. This detailed history should be mandatory reading for any budding Africanist.
174: Don't Save Anything James Salter America North America Non-Fiction Memoir & a Life Examined 2020 2017

Salter's wife put together a collection of his essays and articles and entitled it 'Don't Save Anything'. The title comes from Salter's long time advice 'don't save anything' — meaning don't reserve any writing ideas or details for a later piece, rather pour everything you have into each piece. It's a fitting title representing some of the best writing from Salter, the authors' author. In particular, I was struck by the Salter's terrific profile pieces in the book — I've never read such masterful writing in this genre. Reading them made me wish he'd done biographies. ¶ In the end, writing is like a prison, an island from which you will never be released but which is a kind of paradise: the solitude, the thoughts, the incredible joy of putting into words the essence of what you for the moment understand and with your whole heart want to believe. ¶ You cannot teach someone to write any more than you can teach them to be interesting.
175: Educated Tara Westover America North America Non-Fiction Memoir & a Life Examined 2020 2018

Educated is the story of how one Mormon-ish girl overcomes a childhood under the reign of an undiagnosed bi-polar, off-the-grid father who believed the "end times" are imminent and enforced his own brand of extremist Mormon values upon his family.
176: Lives Other Than My Own Emmanuel Carrère Sri Lanka Asia Non-Fiction Memoir & a Life Examined 2020 2009

In this memoir, French author Emmanuel Carrere takes issue with Fitzgerald's well known assertion that "all life is a process of breaking down" as he peers into the life of Juliette, carefully building a picture of her circling journey from tragedy to love to passion and back to tragedy as her cancer returns to deal its final blow. ¶ That is the worst of fates: never to have been seen, never to have been acknowledged.
177: Mrs. Bridge Evan S. Connell America North America Fiction Sweeping Fiction 2020 1959

With a careful eye and razor sharp bite, author Connell captures a period in American history for the well-heeled social strata, decades before the sexual revolution, feminism, the Vietnam War, and the Civil Rights movement. ¶ This was the night Mrs. Bridge concluded that while marriage might be an equitable affair, love itself was not.
178: She Would Be King Wayétu Moore Liberia Africa Fiction Conflict Zones & Hard Truths 2020 2018

In her debut novel Wayetu Moore channels the idea of lawful magic as she joins magical realist authors like Couto, Martel, and Marquez in telling an alternative origin story of the Pepper Coast lands that would become Liberia.
179: That Will Never Work Marc Randolph America North America Non-Fiction Leadership & Building Things 2020 2019

In this book, equal parts origin story, startup manifesto, and leadership manual, author Marc Randolph recounts how Netflix grew from an idea bandied about in a beaten-up Volvo to a $194B global behemoth.
180: The Art of Fiction James Salter America North America Non-Fiction Memoir & a Life Examined 2020 1983

In his inaugural lecture as a UVA Kapnick Distinguished Writer-in-Residence, Salter offered that "books are passwords"--the idea that among those who are well read, books are a connection, a filial link of brotherhood amidst theretofore strangers. ¶ Books mark a period or place, and then gradually they become that place or time.
181: The Insanity of God ( Nik Ripken Somalia Africa Non-Fiction Christian Faith 2020 2013

At one point author Nikk Ripken's NGO was the ONLY ONE operating in Somalia--his team of 8 was feeding 50,000 refugees a day and running mobile health clinics around the country. ¶ I'd never met a believer in persecution that wasn't running for their life. In those years in Somalia, we had 150 followers of Jesus in the country. When we left, only four were left alive.
182: The Red-Haired Woman Orhan Pamuk Turkey Middle East Fiction Sweeping Fiction 2020 2016

On the surface the novel is about a boy serving as a well apprentice in post-WWII Turkey, two possible murders, one case of possible incest, and late 20th century capitalism in the country. ¶ It seems we would all like a strong, decisive father telling us what to do and what not to do.
183: The Submission Amy Waldman America North America Fiction Sweeping Fiction 2020 2011
This 2011 American Book Award Winner is a backwards look at the psyche and soul of an American public that will never stop grieving 9-11.
184: American Dirt Jeanine Cummins America North America Fiction Sweeping Fiction 2021 2020

This is a brutal, violent, and necessary novel. Author Jeanine Cummins holds nothing back as she pulls the reader into the suffering and anguish that propels countless migrants to make the dangerous journey. ¶ Her body feels like an arrow that's been launched from its bow but hasn't yet found its target.
185: Behold the Dreamers Mbolo Mbue Cameroon Africa Fiction Sweeping Fiction 2021 2016

The novel's power comes in the author's ability to capture both the strengths and the hollowness of the promise of America. The reader sees the rise and good fortune of Jende as his chauffeur position gives him relative wealth and burgeoning opportunities for his family.
186: Born a Crime: Tales from a South African Childhood Trevor Noah South Africa Africa Non-Fiction Conflict Zones & Hard Truths 2021 2016

You may know Trevor Noah as the host of the Daily Show, but long before he entered the mainstream he was a derelict kid born to a black Xhosa mother and a white Swiss father--one who appeared "colored" to those around him but who was raised in the Xhosa culture.
187: Cocktail Hour Under the Tree of Forgetfulness Alexandra Fuller Zambia Africa Non-Fiction Biography Memoir & a Life Examined 2021 2011

Emily appreciated the story's honesty and eye-opening look at both the beauty and sorrow of life. The author shared a unique perspective of a white girl living in Africa during the period of political independence.
188: Homeland Elegies Ayad Akhtar America North America Fiction Sweeping Fiction 2021 2020

Pulitzer-winning author Ayad Akhtar charges that America is a 'buffer solution' that 'keeps things together but always separated' in his unforgettable novel-cum-memoir. DoDReads published my full review. ¶ Constantly defining yourself in opposition to what others say about you is not self-knowledge. It’s confusion.
189: I'm Still Here: Black Dignity in a World Made for Whiteness Austin Channing Brow America North America Non-Fiction Sci-Fi Conflict Zones & Hard Truths 2021 2018

An eye-opening, and heart-opening, look at one woman's experiences growing up and working in "a world made for whiteness." She writes beautifully and with a vulnerability and urgency that asks the reader to wake up and cast aside complacency. ¶ I need a love that is troubled by injustice...a love that has no tolerance for hate, no excuses for racist decisions, no contentment in the status quo.
190: Lion Mountain Mustapha Tlili Tunisia Africa Fiction Sweeping Fiction 2021 1988

In the story, famed Tunisian author Mustapha Tlili paints a secluded village modeled on Feriana, the home of his youth. It's an ancient place lost amidst the desert steppes but which has persisted through the centuries, sheltered always under the shoulder of Lion Mountain. ¶ A geography more than physical or human: sacred...landmarks determining the rights of each and every individual were perfectly clear.
191: Missionaries Phil Klay Colombia South America Fiction War, Service & Sacrifice 2021 2020

Reading Marine veteran Phil Klay's new novel forces readers to step back and consider the 'progress' and globalization of American warfare since 9-11. The novel accomplishes this by examining the decades-long Colombian civil war through the converging lives of a weary American war-zone journalist, an American Special Forces Officer, a career Colombian Army officer, and an orphaned Colombian village boy-turned-killer. DoDReads published my full review. ¶ Wars are not fought by armies. They are fought by cultures. … Your job is not to trim the claws. It’s to kill the beast. ¶ In all his time watching Yemenis die on video screens, he had not once talked to a single Yemeni, or even seen one in person. They were a notional people to him.
192: Project Hail Mary Andy Weir America North America Fiction Sci-Fi & Dystopian 2021 2021

Martian author Andy Weir returns to outer space with a tale that is equal parts nerdy and hokey as he introduces us to Ryland Grace, a failed scientist and reluctant hero. When scientists discover that the sun is slowly being sapped of its power, Grace finds himself in the middle of a race to save earth, and possibly the universe, from extinction.
193: Quiet Cadence Mark Treanor Vietnam Asia Historical Fiction War, Service & Sacrifice 2021 2020
The novel's violence is unrelenting, random, and total. Its first death is a dead body literally flying through the air. ¶ Then the panic hit me: Do I have all my parts?
194: Raising Up a Generation of Third Culture Kids Lauren Wells America North America Non-Fiction Biography Memoir & a Life Examined 2021 2020

While this book is targeted towards parents raising kids overseas, most of it applies to military families. The author posits that kids growing up as "third culture" often end up with enormous amounts of grief and trauma.
195: Steal Away Home: Charles Spurgeon and Thomas Johnson, Unlikely Friends on the Passage to Freedom Matt Carter and Aaron Ivey England, America Europe Non-Fiction Biography Christian Faith 2021 2017

An incredible tale of friendship, faith and sacrifice. Charles Spurgeon is, of course, the renowned "prince of preachers." Authors Matt Carter and Aaron Ivey tell the story of his friendship with African-American missionary Thomas Johnson against the backdrop of Spurgeon's own struggles with depression, anxiety and gout.
196: Talking to Strangers Malcolm Gladwell America North America Non-Fiction Leadership & Building Things 2021 2019

As a society we are not equipped to talk to strangers, so when things don't go as expected we blame the stranger as our immediate reflex. Instead we need to recognize our own limits to decipher and truly understand strangers, and instead embrace humility and restraint.
197: The Anomaly Hervé Le Tellier Multiple Europe Fiction Sweeping Fiction 2021 2020

I first heard about this novel in a NYT article that mentioned the now available translation of the book that had enraptured France during the COVID lockdowns. The premise is that there's some sort of time-continuum split where a flight lands with the same people and same plane that had landed months earlier.
198: The Desert and the Drum Mbarek Ould Beyrouk Mauritania Africa Fiction Sweeping Fiction 2021 2015

"From the moment they arrived, the strangers stole something essential from us, without us feeling we had the right to protest." This comment by the young Bedouin narrator Rayhana encapsulates the modern-day struggle that Mauritanian author Mbarek Ould Beyrouk seeks to describe. ¶ From the moment they arrived, the strangers stole something essential from us, without us feeling we had the right to protest.
199: The Dissent Channel Elizabeth Shackleford Sudan/South Sudan Africa Non-Fiction Conflict Zones & Hard Truths 2021 2020
During a Famous Rivers Africa Group session, we discussed this memoir with the author Lizzy Shackleton.
200: The Promise Damon Galgut South Africa Africa Fiction Sweeping Fiction 2021 2021

Of course one isn't awarded the Booker prize for penning a surface-level story about a white family in South Africa. Rather Galgut has written a soaring multi-decade exposition on the promise of a post-Apartheid South Africa writ large.
201: What the Day Owes the Night Yasmina Khadra Algeria Africa Fiction Sweeping Fiction 2021 2008

This book is a perfect example of why reading fiction is important. Reading fiction like this forces the reader to internalize and grapple with historical events in a way that a straightforward history never could. In this case, by personalizing something like the Algerian independence struggle, the reader must reevaluate the dry numbers, facts and statistics littering the historical record and connect them to the actual people and struggles behind them. ¶ Have you ever dared, Younes, even once in your life? ¶ If a woman loves you, no star is beyond your grasp, no god can touch you. ¶ Only love can make good the misfortunes and evils of the world.
202: A Caring Life Aaron Santymire Multiple Africa Non-Fiction Christian Faith 2022 2020

I met author Aaron Santymire during my first embassy tour in Madagascar, where he served as a medical missionary. He's spent his entire adult life serving and caring for his family on the African continent, and this beautiful book is the accumulated outpouring of his wisdom.
203: An Italian Education Tiim Parks Italy Europe Non-Fiction Memoir & a Life Examined 2022 1996

Published a quarter of a century ago, many of Tim Parks' observations still ring true in 2022 Italy. Chocked full of short vignettes that capture a Brit's experience raising his bi-national children in fair Verona. ¶ Stessa spiaggia, stesso mare.
204: How Beautiful We Were Mbolo Mbue Cameroon Africa Fiction Sweeping Fiction 2022 2021

"The problem with America is that it makes you dream"--this may well have been the last unspoken dying sigh of Thula, the protagonist in this second novel from Imbolo Mbue. ¶ The problem with America is that it makes you dream.
205: In the Name of Jesus: Reflections on Christian Leadership Henri J.M. Nouwen Netherlands Europe Non-Fiction Christian Christian Faith 2022 1989

Father Henri Nouwen taught for 20 years at Harvard, Notre Dame, and Yale but began to feel his own spiritual death developing--what many Christian leaders may identify as burnout. So he prayed a simple, but very brave, prayer. ¶ Lord, show me where you want me to go and I will follow you, but please be clear and unambiguous about it!
206: Let My People Go Surfing: The Education of a Reluctant Businessman Yvon Chouinard America North America Non-Fiction Leadership & Building Things 2022 2005

Today everyone knows the name Patagonia, and on a cold winter day you can't go too far without seeing the familiar logo on someone's sweater. But nearly 50 years ago the global company was just what we'd today call a side hustle. ¶ Maintaining a sense of urgency throughout a company is one of the most difficult challenges in business.
207: SuperNova Era Ciu Lixin China Asia Science Fiction Sci-Fi & Dystopian 2022 2003

While not as polished and developed as his later works, I tore through this quick-paced narrative in two days. The premise is intriguing--a supernova event occurs that kills off the entire adult population in a matter of months.
208: Taste: My Life Through Food Stanley Tucci America North America Non-Fiction Memoir & a Life Examined 2022 2021

This is Stanley Tucci's life told against the backdrop of food--it brought to mind another truly great food memoir, Life is Meals by James and Kay Salter, my favorite book by my favorite author to give as a housewarming gift.
209: The Fortune Men Nadifa Mohamed Somalia Africa Historical Fiction Conflict Zones & Hard Truths 2022 2021

"Somalis have got the right idea, you wrong someone and you're forced to look over your shoulder for the rest of your life unless you make amends. You deal with each other face to face. Only cowards live by prisons and cold hangings." ¶ You wrong someone and you're forced to look over your shoulder for the rest of your life unless you make amends. Only cowards live by prisons and cold hangings.
